At beginner level, people learn that SEO helps a business "show up on Google". At professional level, a client or employer asks a harder question: **how much is better search visibility worth to us, and where should we start?** This lesson teaches you to answer that question with the website's own data instead of guesses or borrowed industry figures.

The four numbers that connect search to money

Every search visit passes through the same chain. Google shows a page in results (an **impression**). Some searchers click (**clicks**, and clicks divided by impressions is the **click-through rate** or CTR, as Search Console defines it). Some of those visitors take a valuable action such as an order, a quote request or a booking (**conversions**). Each conversion is worth some amount to the business (**value per conversion**).

Impressions in Search Console
Clicks (impressions x CTR)
Visits in analytics
Conversions (visits x rate)
Revenue (conversions x value)
Each step multiplies by a rate you can measure on the client's own site, so the estimate is grounded in their reality.

Impressions, clicks, CTR and average position come from **Google Search Console**, in the Performance report. The conversion rate comes from the client's analytics (for example Google Analytics 4) or, for small businesses, from their own order book or WhatsApp records. Value per conversion comes from the owner: average order value for a shop, or average job value for a service firm.
Step one: split branded and non-branded demand

**Branded queries** contain the business name, for example "Zara Fabrics Lagos". People searching these already know the business, so the site usually ranks first anyway. **Non-branded queries** describe a need, for example "ankara fabric wholesale lagos". These are where SEO creates new customers. In the Performance report, add a query filter that excludes the brand name and its common misspellings, then note total non-branded impressions and clicks. If non-branded clicks are tiny compared with branded clicks, the site is mostly being found by people who already know it, which is itself a key finding for the client.

Step two: find striking-distance queries

A page sitting at average position 8 to 20 for a relevant query is said to be in **striking distance**: Google already considers it relevant, but it is just below the results most people click. Improving that page (its title, its content depth, its internal links) is usually faster than ranking a brand-new page from nothing. Sort the non-branded queries by impressions, then keep the ones with an average position between roughly 8 and 20 and clear commercial intent. Open the Pages tab for each to see which URL is ranking.
Average position is an average

Search Console reports the average of the topmost position your site held each time it appeared. A value of 11.4 can hide days at position 6 and days at position 20. Look at the trend over several weeks before you treat a query as stable.
Step three: use the site's own CTR, not internet averages

You will find many published "CTR by position" charts online. They come from different studies, different countries and different years, and they rarely match a specific site. A more honest method is to look at the client's own queries that already rank in positions 3 to 5 and calculate their average CTR. That becomes your assumption for what a moved query might achieve. Then always build two cases: an optimistic one using that CTR, and a conservative one using half of it.
Worked example: is one query worth the work?

For example, Kemi sells ankara and lace online from Lagos and asks whether SEO is worth paying for. Her Search Console data for the last three months shows the non-branded query "ankara fabric wholesale lagos" with 12,000 impressions, 96 clicks and an average position of 11.4. Her queries that already sit in positions 3 to 5 average a 6% CTR. Her analytics show 1.5% of organic visitors place an order, and her average order is about 45,000 naira (approximate, from her own records).
Optimistic case: 12,000 x 6% = 720 clicks. Extra clicks: 720 - 96 = 624.
Extra orders: 624 x 1.5% = 9.36, about 9 orders in three months.
Extra revenue: 9.36 x 45,000 = 421,200 naira (approximate).
Conservative case: CTR of 3% gives 360 clicks, so 264 extra clicks, 3.96 extra orders and about 178,200 naira over three months.
She records both figures, the assumptions behind them and the date range used.

Kemi now knows this one query could be worth roughly 178,000 to 421,000 naira of extra sales per quarter if the page reaches the top five. That range, not a guarantee, tells her the page deserves attention first.

Clients and developers judge an SEO professional by how precisely she speaks. Every time a browser or Googlebot requests a URL, the server answers with a three-digit **status code** before sending any content. You can see it in Search Console's URL Inspection tool, in a crawler such as Screaming Frog, or in your browser's developer tools.

Redirects: permanent or temporary

Google's documentation separates redirects into two families. **Permanent** redirects (301, 308, and an instant meta refresh) tell Google the new URL should replace the old one in results. **Temporary** redirects (302, 303, 307) are followed, but Google may keep the old URL indexed. Use a permanent redirect when you are sure it will not be reverted, for example after moving a site from http to https. Google also prefers **server-side** redirects; JavaScript redirects only work if Google successfully renders the page.

A **redirect chain** is when URL A redirects to B, which redirects to C. Each extra hop slows visitors and wastes crawling. Search Console reports a "Redirect error" when a chain is too long or loops. The professional fix is to point every old URL straight at the final destination in one hop.
Duplicate URLs and canonicalisation

The same page often lives at several addresses: with and without https, with and without www, and with tracking parameters such as ?utm_source=whatsapp or ?gclid=. Google groups these duplicates and picks one **canonical** URL to show in results. You influence that choice with signals. In Google's own order of strength: a **redirect** is a strong signal, a **rel="canonical"** link in the page head is a strong signal, and listing a URL in the **XML sitemap** is a weak signal. Use them together and make sure they agree.
Put a self-referencing canonical tag on every canonical page, with an absolute URL (https://www.example.com/page, not /page).
Link internally to the canonical version only.
List only canonical URLs in the sitemap.
Do not use robots.txt, the URL removal tool or noindex to choose a canonical; Google advises against all three for this purpose.
Worked example: one homepage, five addresses

For example, Halima manages the website of an events company in Kaduna. A crawl shows the homepage answering at http://eventsco.ng, http://www.eventsco.ng, https://eventsco.ng, https://www.eventsco.ng and https://www.eventsco.ng/?utm_source=whatsapp. Search Console marks some as "Duplicate without user-selected canonical".
She chooses https://www.eventsco.ng/ as the canonical, because most backlinks already point there.
She tests each variant and finds http://eventsco.ng goes to https://eventsco.ng, then to https://www.eventsco.ng: a chain of two hops.
She asks the developer for one server-side 301 rule so every http and non-www variant goes straight to https://www.eventsco.ng/ in a single hop.
The UTM version stays live (the WhatsApp campaign needs it) but gets a canonical tag pointing to https://www.eventsco.ng/.
She checks that the sitemap and the site menu use only the canonical URL, then re-tests with URL Inspection.

Four variants now redirect in one hop, the tracking URL consolidates by canonical tag, and all signals agree. Halima logs the change with the date so she can check the Page indexing report two to four weeks later.

This confusion appears in many audits. Search Console even has a warning status, "Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt", for pages Google indexed from links without being allowed to crawl them. If the goal is "keep this out of search results", use noindex and let Google crawl the page.
Rendering and structured data in one paragraph each

**Rendering** is Google running a page's JavaScript to see the final content, much as a browser does. If important text, links or canonical tags only appear after scripts run, they may be seen late or not at all. Google recommends putting canonical tags in the HTML source rather than adding them by script. Compare "view source" with the rendered HTML in URL Inspection when you suspect a problem.

**Structured data** is code, usually in JSON-LD format, that labels page content for search engines: an organisation's name and logo, a product's price, an event's date. It can make a page eligible for richer result features, but it is not a promise of them, and it must describe content that visitors can actually see on the page.
Core Web Vitals thresholds

For page experience, web.dev lists good scores as Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024.

Mobile-first and data-conscious audiences

Google uses the mobile version of a site for indexing and ranking, so whatever is missing on mobile is effectively missing for Google. In Nigerian and many other African markets, most visitors browse on smartphones and pay for data by the bundle. Practical consequences: compress images and serve modern formats such as WebP, avoid auto-playing video, keep key text and contact details in the HTML rather than inside images, and test pages on a mid-range Android phone over mobile data, not only on office Wi-Fi.

hreflang: telling Google which version is for whom

When pages exist in different languages, or in the same language for different countries, the **hreflang** annotation tells Google which version to show to which searcher. Google accepts it in three equivalent places: link tags in the HTML head, HTTP headers, or the XML sitemap. The rules from Google's documentation that most often catch people out:
The code is a language code in ISO 639-1 format, optionally followed by a region code in ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 format: en-NG, en-GH, en-GB.
A region alone is invalid: "NG" will not work, it must be "en-NG".
"UK" is not a valid region code; the United Kingdom is GB, so use en-GB.
Every version must list itself and all the others. If two pages do not point to each other, the annotations are ignored.
x-default marks the fallback page for searchers who match none of the listed versions, often a country selector or the main international page.
Worked example: hreflang for a skincare brand in three markets

For example, Ifeoma's skincare brand sells from Lagos. Her shea body butter has three versions: brand.com/ng/shea-butter (naira prices, Lagos and Abuja delivery), brand.com/gh/shea-butter (cedi prices, Accra delivery) and brand.com/uk/shea-butter (pound prices, UK shipping). She also has brand.com/shea-butter for everyone else.
She maps each URL to a code: /ng/ is en-NG, /gh/ is en-GH, /uk/ is en-GB (not en-UK), and the general page is x-default.
She writes four link tags, for example: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-GB" href="https://brand.com/uk/shea-butter" />, one for each version including x-default.
She places the same set of four tags in the head of all four pages, so each page references itself and the other three: 4 pages x 4 tags = 16 tags in total.
She checks that each version has a self-referencing canonical tag, not a canonical pointing to the Nigerian page, because a canonical to another country page would tell Google to drop that version.
She crawls the four URLs with Screaming Frog's free version, which reports missing return links in its hreflang checks.
A searcher in Accra is more likely to see the cedi page and one in London the pound page, and Google no longer treats the three country pages as competing duplicates.
Language codes for local languages

Hausa (ha), Yoruba (yo), Igbo (ig) and Swahili (sw) have two-letter ISO 639-1 codes. Nigerian Pidgin does not have a two-letter ISO 639-1 code, so check Google's current hreflang documentation before tagging Pidgin pages rather than inventing a code.
Translation is not localisation

Machine-translating a page into Yoruba or French and publishing it rarely helps. Real localisation changes prices and currency, delivery and payment options (Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint for Nigerian buyers, for instance), phone formats, examples and the words local people actually search. Do keyword research separately for each market: Ghanaian and Nigerian shoppers may use different words for the same product.

URL Inspection: the single most useful check

Paste any URL from the property into the inspection bar at the top of Search Console. You see whether the URL is on Google, which canonical Google selected, whether it was crawled as a smartphone, and the last crawl date. **Test live URL** fetches the page now, so you can compare the live version with what Google has stored. The Page indexing report: triage, do not panic

This report groups every known URL into indexed and not indexed, with a reason for each. Large "not indexed" numbers frighten clients, but many reasons are normal. Your job is to ask one question of each reason: **does this group contain pages the business needs in search?**

Crawl politely

A crawler can send many requests quickly. On small shared hosting, lower the crawl speed in the configuration so you do not slow the client's site for real customers, and always crawl only sites you have permission to audit.
Field data and lab data

PageSpeed Insights shows two kinds of results. **Field data** comes from real Chrome users over the previous 28 days and is what the Core Web Vitals assessment uses, judged at the 75th percentile. **Lab data** is a single Lighthouse test from Google's servers under set conditions. They often disagree. If field data is good but lab data is poor, real visitors are fine and the lab test is simply harsher; if field data is poor, real customers are suffering and it belongs in the audit. Small sites may have no field data at all, because not enough Chrome users visited; then you rely on lab data and on testing with a real phone.
Structured data and Bing

Run key templates (homepage, a product or service page, an article) through the Rich Results Test to see which result features the page is eligible for, and through the Schema Markup Validator to check the schema itself. Finally, add the site to Bing Webmaster Tools, which can import properties directly from Search Console. Bing powers results in some other services too, and its site scan is a useful second check.

**Baseline snapshot:** export three to sixteen months of Search Console data, organic conversions from analytics, and a full crawl, all dated.

**Score and prioritise:** give every finding the same score (below).
**Tickets and implementation:** turn top findings into tickets for the developer, writer or owner.
**Verify and report:** confirm each fix is live and measure it (next lesson).
Critical blockers come first

Some issues stop a site from appearing in search at all. Check for these before scoring anything else: a sitewide noindex left over from development, a robots.txt line "Disallow: /" blocking everything, canonical tags pointing to a staging or old domain, the whole site returning server errors, or the https version redirecting back to http. These go to the top of the list with the label **critical** and are reported to the client the same day.
The staging leftover

When developers copy a site from a test server, settings such as noindex or canonicals to the test domain sometimes come with it. After any site launch or redesign, check the homepage source and URL Inspection immediately.
Scoring with Impact x Confidence x Ease

Give each finding three scores from 1 to 5. **Impact**: how much it could change visibility or conversions for pages the business cares about. **Confidence**: how sure you are, based on evidence, that fixing it will help. **Ease**: how easy it is to implement (5 is very easy). Multiply them. The maximum is 5 x 5 x 5 = 125. The score is not science; its value is that it makes your reasoning visible and consistent, and the client can challenge a single number instead of the whole plan.

E. No Organization structured data: 1 x 3 x 5 = 15.

Her order is A (125, also a critical blocker), B (48), F (40), D (24), C (18), E (15). The slow pages matter, but they need a developer and more time, so they come after quicker, high-confidence fixes.

A recommendation is not a result. Between your ticket and a real improvement, many things can go wrong: a fix applied to one page instead of the template, a cache that still serves the old version, or a traffic rise that was really a seasonal spike. Quality assurance protects the client and your reputation.
A person checking data with a magnifying glass and tick marks
Verify that each change is live before you measure whether it worked.
Three checks that a fix is live

**Source check:** open view source on two or three affected pages and confirm the exact change, for example the new title or the corrected canonical. Check on a phone too, because some sites serve different HTML to mobile.
**Recrawl:** run the same crawler settings as your baseline and compare counts: duplicate titles, broken links or noindex pages should have fallen to the expected number.

**Google's view:** use URL Inspection with Test live URL on key pages. For issues listed in the Page indexing report, click Validate fix. Google's help pages say validation typically takes up to about two weeks and will email you as it progresses.
Caching can fool you
Many WordPress sites use caching plugins or a service such as Cloudflare. If the change does not show, ask the developer to clear the cache before you report the fix as failed.
Measuring change honestly

When the fix is live, wait long enough for Google to recrawl and for data to build up, often several weeks for small sites. Then compare **equal-length periods** with the same mix of weekdays: for example 28 days before the change against 28 days after, skipping the first days while Google was still recrawling. Search Console's Performance report can compare two date ranges directly.
Next, look for things other than your change that could explain the difference:
**Seasonality:** compare with the same period last year if data exists. School-related searches, festive shopping and rainy-season services all rise and fall.
**Google updates:** check the Google Search Status Dashboard for ranking updates announced during your window.
**Other site changes:** ask whether prices, products, ads or social campaigns changed.
**A comparison group:** pick similar pages you did not change and see how they moved over the same dates.

Worked example: did the new titles work?

For example, Chioma rewrote titles and meta descriptions on 8 recipe pages of a Nigerian food blog. She compared 28 days before with 28 days after, leaving out the week of the change. She kept 10 similar recipe pages unchanged as a comparison group.
Before: 18,400 impressions, 331 clicks. CTR = 331 / 18,400 = 1.80%. Average position 6.2.
After: 19,100 impressions, 516 clicks. CTR = 516 / 19,100 = 2.70%. Average position 6.0.
Relative CTR change: 2.70 / 1.80 is about 1.50, so CTR rose by about 50%.
Comparison group CTR moved from 2.1% to 2.2%, a relative rise of about 4.8%.
Position barely moved (6.2 to 6.0), and the Status Dashboard showed no announced update in either window.

Because position was stable and the untouched pages hardly changed, the CTR jump is most likely due to the new titles. Chioma reports it as "strong evidence", not proof, and plans to recheck after another 28 days.
The change log

Two cautions about the arithmetic. First, distinguish **percentage points** from **percent**: a CTR moving from 1.80% to 2.70% is a rise of 0.9 percentage points, which is a relative rise of about 50%. Say which one you mean, because clients often confuse them. Second, small numbers swing wildly. A page going from 4 clicks to 8 clicks has "doubled", but that difference could easily be chance, so group similar pages together before drawing conclusions.

Discovery is where SEO projects succeed or fail. If you do not know which enquiries actually make the client money, you will optimise the wrong pages. Google's own advice to business owners hiring an SEO suggests they ask whether the SEO is interested in understanding their business, competitors and customers. Your discovery call is where you show that you are.

Discovery call checklist

Cover all five before you promise any deliverable.
**Goals:** What does a good month look like? Which services or products bring the most profit? How do enquiries arrive: website form, phone, WhatsApp, walk-in?
**Customers:** Who buys? What words do they use when they call? Ask for five recent enquiries (with personal details removed) and note their phrasing.
**History:** Has anyone done SEO before? Was the site redesigned, moved to a new domain or rebuilt recently? Has traffic ever dropped suddenly?
**Competitors:** Who do they lose jobs to? Then search the main services yourself on a phone and note who actually ranks, which may be different.
**Constraints:** Monthly budget, who can edit the website and how many hours they have, and any dates such as a product launch or a busy season.
Ask about tracking early

Many small businesses cannot say how many enquiries came from Google. Ask how they record enquiries now. If the answer is "we don't", setting up a simple record (a form notification, a phone log or a "how did you find us" question) becomes part of the first month's work.
Getting access the safe way

Never ask a client for their Google password. Search Console and Google Analytics both let owners add other people with their own Google accounts. In Search Console, an owner adds you under Settings, then Users and permissions. Google defines three levels: **owners** can manage users and settings, **full users** can view all data and take most actions, and **restricted users** have limited viewing. For most audits, ask for **full user**. Ownership should stay with the client, so they never lose control of their own property if you stop working together.

Analytics, contact forms and CRM exports can contain names, phone numbers and emails. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 governs how personal data is processed in Nigeria. Every number in Ngozi's proposal traces back to hours and a rate she chose, so she can explain it calmly if the client asks for a discount, and reduce scope rather than simply cutting the price.
What a proposal contains
**Summary of their goal** in their words, taken from the confirmed brief.
**Deliverables** with dates, for example "Audit report and scored 90-day roadmap, delivered by 30 June; 60-minute presentation call".
**Inclusions:** the pages, templates or number of URLs covered.
**Exclusions:** what is not included, such as writing new content, link building, paid ads, or development work.
**Client responsibilities:** access within three working days, a named contact, and developer time for fixes.
**Price, payment terms and validity** (for example, valid for 30 days).
**What results to expect:** realistic, with no ranking guarantee, and the indicator you will report on.
**Change requests and ending the agreement:** how extra work is priced and how either side can end a retainer with notice.
Never sell guarantees or shortcuts

Do not promise positions ("page one in 30 days") and do not include purchased links or automated content in a package. Google's spam policies prohibit buying links to manipulate rankings and mass-producing low-value pages, and the client's site, not yours, carries the risk.
Controlling scope during the work

Scope creep usually arrives politely: "While you're in there, could you also rewrite the About page?" Answer warmly and in writing. Confirm the request is outside the agreed scope, give its estimated hours and cost, and ask whether to add it now, swap it for something in the current scope, or leave it for later. Record the decision. A short change request like this, sent on WhatsApp or email, keeps the relationship friendly and your hours paid.
Write the swap option
Offering to swap a new request for an existing task of similar size helps clients with fixed budgets say yes without feeling pressured to spend more.
A change request in practice

Suppose the bookshop owner asks Ngozi to also review 15 blog posts during the audit. Ngozi estimates 15 minutes per post, so 15 x 15 = 225 minutes, about 4 hours. Her message reads: "Happy to help with the blog posts. They are outside the audit scope we agreed. Reviewing all 15 would take about 4 hours, which is 40,000 naira at our agreed rate. We can add it now, swap it for the presentation call and a shorter written walkthrough, or schedule it for the first retainer month. Which would you prefer?" The owner chooses the retainer month, and Ngozi records the decision in the project notes. Nobody feels cheated, and the audit still arrives on time.

Protect your cash flow in the same written way. Send invoices with a clear due date, start work only after the agreed first payment arrives, and pause extra work, politely, when an invoice is overdue. For retainers, invoice at the start of each month, not the end.

At beginner level, you learn that SEO helps a business show up on Google.

The money chain
Four numbers connect search to money
Impressions: Google shows the page in results
Clicks: some searchers click (CTR = clicks / impressions)
Conversions: some visitors order, book or ask for a quote
Value per conversion: what each one is worth
Every search visit passes through the same chain. First, Google shows a page in results. That is an impression.
Some searchers click. Clicks divided by impressions is the click-through rate, or CTR. You find these numbers in Search Console, in the Performance report.
Some visitors take a valuable action, like an order, a booking or a quote request. That is a conversion.
Finally, each conversion is worth some amount. The owner tells you the average order or job value.
Step by step
Sizing the opportunity
Filter out branded queries
Keep non-branded queries at position 8 to 20
Use the site's own CTR for positions 3 to 5
Build an optimistic and a conservative case
Give a range with your working. Never promise a ranking.
Step one. Remove branded queries, the ones with the business name. People searching those already know the business. Non-branded queries describe a need, and that is where SEO wins new customers.
Step two. Find striking-distance queries, at an average position of about 8 to 20. Google already sees the page as relevant, so improving it is usually the faster win.
Step three. Do not use CTR charts from the internet. Look at the client's own queries in positions 3 to 5 and use their average CTR.
Step four. Build two cases. An optimistic one with that CTR, and a conservative one with half of it.
Google's own guidance says no one can guarantee a number one ranking. So label your estimate as a scenario, show the inputs and the formula, and give both cases.

Speak precisely
Status codes you will meet
200: OK, the page can be indexed
301 or 308: moved permanently
302 or 307: temporary redirect
404: not found, fix internal links to it
5xx: server error, Google cannot read it
Developers judge you by how precisely you speak. Every server answers with a three-digit status code. 200 means OK.
301 and 308 are permanent. Google treats the new address as the main one.
302 and 307 are temporary. Google follows them but may keep the old address.
404 means not found. 5xx means a server error. And point every old address straight to the final one in one hop, with no redirect chains.
Common mistake
Use for endless filter pages
noindex
Never also block it in robots.txt
A Disallow line in robots.txt stops Google fetching a page, but the page can still be indexed from links.
A noindex tag keeps a page out of results, but Google must crawl the page to see it. So if you want a page out of search, use noindex and let Google crawl it.
Your market
A clinic, school or caterer in one city. Local search, fast mobile pages, plain language.
A Lagos brand selling in Ghana and the UK. Country targeting and hreflang.
A company abroad. Technical audits at scale and clear written reports.
You can work in three markets. Local businesses need local search, simple sites and fast pages on modest phones, because most visitors pay for data by the bundle.
Multi-country brands need hreflang, which tells Google which version is for which country. Use valid codes like en-NG and en-GB, never en-UK, and every version must list itself and all the others.
Remote international clients need technical audits at scale and clear written reports. Many people start local, then add remote work later.

Confidence: how sure the evidence makes you
